headline: $200 billion a year for nature. Less than half showed up.
summary: In 2022, nearly 200 countries agreed in Montreal to protect 30% of the world's land and water by 2030, and to raise $200 billion a year to pay for it. They are raising $75 to $92 billion. A UN report out Thursday puts the land on track for 26%, the sea for 12%. Talks open Monday in Yerevan, Armenia. The US is not in the treaty.
cover_answer: Everyone is short. The US isn't even in the treaty.
table_question: You promise to save up and only get halfway. Did you break it?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Almost 200 countries made a promise to keep nature safe: about a third of the land and the sea, for the animals and the trees. Picture a big jar with a line near the top, and every country dropping coins in. Right now the jar is less than half full. Next week the grown-ups meet in a city called Yerevan to work on filling it.
5-7.why: A jar with a line on it. The promise and the shortfall in one picture a six-year-old can hold.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the money, which they cannot see, becomes a jar with a line near the top and coins going in. Piaget's point: the amount has to be a thing before it can be an idea. Expect "which animals?" The article names rays and sharks in the Philippines, so start there.

8-12.script: Nearly 200 countries signed a checklist for nature in 2022: protect 30% of land and sea by 2030, raise $200 billion a year to pay for it. The UN checked the list Thursday. Fewer than half the targets are on track, and the money is under half the goal. Monday they meet in Armenia.
8-12.why: Checklist, deadline, report. A chain they follow, then ask who is behind.
8-12.why_long: Eight-to-twelve-year-olds are working out whether adults keep the rules they set, so the script hands them the checklist and the check: 23 targets, a deadline, a report that says fewer than half are on track. Expect "what happens to the countries that didn't do it?" The article doesn't say. The meeting is where they find out.

13-17.script: If 200 countries promise $200 billion a year and bring in under half, is that failure or progress? The UN says 26% of land and 12% of sea by 2030, against 30%. Second: the US isn't in the treaty at all. Does staying out make it blameless, or just absent?
13-17.why: One number read two ways, and a country that opted out. They can hold both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: $75 to $92 billion a year is a lot of money, and less than half the promise. Kuhn's finding is that argument is practised against someone honest, so the script leaves the US question open. Expect "why isn't the US in it?" The article doesn't say. Don't guess.

5-7.a: Lots. The story names rays and sharks in the Philippines, and a huge wet grassland in Cambodia that is now protected.

8-12.a: Parks cost money. Poor countries were promised $20 billion a year.
Some. Latin America: 29% of its land. Oceania: 41% of its seas.

13-17.a: Everyone is short, under half the goal. The US isn't in the treaty at all.

13-17.q: Does a promise like this mean anything?
13-17.a: Some. Latin America has committed 29% of its land, Oceania 41% of its seas.
